claims.text: The initial CoCrFeMnNi alloy is single-phase, chemically homogeneous, and has a uniform microstructure.
Service-like stresses at moderate temperatures can induce localized intragranular chemical ordering or spinodal decomposition in single-phase CoCrFeMnNi.
Stress-assisted diffusion and local compositional fluctuations produce nanoscale ordered domains within grain interiors.
Under low-strain-rate, moderate-temperature loading, local compositional fluctuations become thermodynamically favorable.
The favorable compositional fluctuations trigger intragranular ordering or spinodal decomposition.
Nanoscale ordered domains impede dislocation motion.
Nanoscale ordered domains locally concentrate stress.
The ordered domains act as crack-nucleation sites within grain interiors.
Intragranular crack initiation caused by ordered domains reduces toughness independently of grain-boundary effects.
Low strain rates at room to moderately elevated temperatures favor stress-assisted diffusion and ordering.
High strain rates at cryogenic temperatures suppress diffusion and intragranular ordering.
Diffusion-favorable loading will produce nanoscale intragranular ordered precipitates detectable by TEM or APT.
Diffusion-favorable loading will reduce toughness relative to the initial single-phase baseline.
Diffusion-favorable loading will shift crack initiation toward grain interiors.
High-strain-rate or cryogenic tests will retain baseline toughness and show no intragranular ordering features.
The proposed mechanism should dominate at moderate temperatures and low-to-intermediate strain rates where diffusion is active.
The comparison between low-rate moderate-temperature loading and high-rate cryogenic loading isolates the effect of stress-induced nanoscale ordering.

Failure to detect intragranular ordering under diffusion-favorable loading, or failure to associate toughness degradation with intragranular rather than grain-boundary cracking, would reject the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The comparison is said to isolate stress-induced ordering while simultaneously changing both strain rate and temperature. Those coupled changes prevent attribution to either stress-assisted diffusion, strain rate, or temperature alone.

APT is described as an in-situ, real-time monitoring method, whereas the proposed design also treats it as a technique for monitoring domains during deformation; conventional APT is generally destructive and post-mortem rather than real-time, making the stated measurement mode internally methodologically inconsistent.
